## KEY MESSAGES

Key Message 1

Annual average temperatures in Virginia have increased more than 1.5°F since the beginning of the 20th century. The state has warmed rapidly since the 1970s, and 2015–2024 was the warmest decade on record. Under the intermediate and higher emissions pathways, historically unprecedented warming is projected during this century, with associated increases in heat wave intensity and decreases in cold wave intensity.

Key Message 2

Annual precipitation has been trending upward since the 1970s, largely driven by increases in summer precipitation. Extreme precipitation events have been near or above average since the 1990s and are projected to become more frequent and intense.

Key Message 3

Virginia is at considerable risk from sea level rise because of its extensive shoreline, low coastal elevation, and coastal subsidence (sinking). The state’s sea levels rose by about 10 inches between 1970 and 2020. Projections under the Intermediate sea level scenario show an additional rise of about 12 inches by 2050 and 1.8 feet by 2070. High-tide flood events have become more frequent in recent years, and further increases are expected as sea levels continue to rise.

Virginia has a humid climate with very warm summers and moderately cold winters. There is substantial regional variation in climate due to the state's diverse geographic features, which include the Appalachian and Blue Ridge Mountains in the west and the Atlantic coastal region in the east. Temperature and precipitation patterns are highly influenced by these geographic features, and the west and north tend to be cooler and drier than the eastern coastal region. Winter low temperatures range from the low 20s (°F) at high elevations to more than 35°F along the coast ([1991–2020 averages]). Summer high temperatures range from around 80°F in the Appalachians to around 90°F in the far southeast. Virginia summers are often humid, with frequent thunderstorms in the afternoons and evenings. Rainfall amounts are generally higher east of the Blue Ridge Mountains and lower to the west. For example, annual precipitation is less than 40 inches in the Shenandoah Valley, compared to around 50 inches along the tidewater coastal region. Some high-elevation locations, however, receive more than 55 inches per year. Annual snowfall totals range from more than 45 inches in the Appalachian Mountains to less than 10 inches along the coastal plain and parts of southern Virginia.

## Average Winter Daytime Temperature in Richmond Virginia

The typical winter daytime high in Richmond, Virginia runs in the upper 40s to low 50s°F, with the overall winter average around 42-43°F. Recent years have been warmer than historical norms, with 2023 setting a record as Richmond’s warmest year since 1897 and winter temperatures averaging about 3.7°F higher than in 1970.

Typical Winter Daytime Highs and Monthly Averages

Richmond’s winter climate is classified as humid subtropical, with cool rather than frigid winters. Daytime highs usually sit in the 40s and 50s during December through February, though swings are common. The city’s average December temperature has climbed from 38.6° in the late 1890s to 42.3° in 2022, and January is climatologically about 3.5° colder than December.

[**Ben Vickers** Posted in The Richmond Boys Richmond has a Warm Temperate Climate and a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa), with hot and humid summers and generally cool winters. 3]

[![Image 3: Post media preview] **LSA Weather Perspectives** Temperatures will reach the 40s to low 50s Saturday and 30s to low 40s Sunday. 10 2]

Recent Winter Trends and Record Warmth

Winter in Richmond has been warming noticeably. The 2022-2023 winter ranked as the #3 warmest on record, and 2023 was officially the warmest year since records began in 1897 with an annual average of 61.3°F. Climate data shows winter is the fastest warming season locally, up 3.7°F since 1970. Even so, cold snaps still happen — January 2025 averaged 30.4°F, about 7.8° below normal and the coldest January in decades.

[![Image 8: Post media preview] **Sean Sublette, Meteorologist** For ease of record keeping, we define winter as Dec-Feb: the climatologically 3 coldest months of the year. 16 1]

Cold Snaps and Temperature Swings

While averages are mild, Richmond can see sharp cold periods and big day-to-day swings. A polar outbreak in 1985 brought a record low of -6°F, and January 2018 dropped to -3°F. More recently, temperatures fell to 15°F in January and 28°F in mid-December. Locals often joke that you can experience all four seasons in 48 hours — one day it’s 88°F, the next it’s snowing.

Snowfall and Winter Conditions

Snow isn’t a given in Richmond. The average seasonal snowfall is just over 8 inches, and totals are usually boosted by one big storm. The last 10 years have averaged 8.7 inches from December through March. Some winters pass with little to no snow, and when it does fall it’s often slushy and melts quickly as temperatures hover near freezing.
